extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers and meta-analysts in health / biomedical research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for methods to prevent, detect, and mitigate publication and related dissemination biases when conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in health research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing formats (printed+supplementary vs electronic-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of electronic publishing: printed journals with electronic supplementary materials, and electronic only journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electronic formats (e.g. Trial Bank Model, BMJ 'electronic long–paper short' ELPS) to publish additional data and longer methodological information that would aid transparency and reduce reporting bias. Electronic publication provides unlimited space, linkage between references, timely publication, and cost-effective dissemination and archiving; but electronic publishing alone cannot resolve biased publication/reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing peer-review reports alongside articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review in the context of electronic publishing remains important and can be published in conjunction with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some online BioMed journals publish accepted papers with their initially submitted versions and comments from peer-reviewers plus responses from authors. Publishing peer-review materials increases transparency about review process and changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals for negative results
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals dedicated to publishing studies with negative results can be a specific remedy for publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Negative Results in Biomedicine (open access, indexed by MEDLINE/EMBASE/Scopus/Google Scholar) increases retrievability of negative results for systematic reviewers. Such journals improve visibility of non-significant findings but have had limited output to date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about pay-to-publish open access models
rubrics_metrics.description: Many online open access journals charge authors a fee to cover publishing costs, and the impact of this pay-to-publish model on publication bias and study quality is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that author-pays models may introduce selection pressures or affect quality; monitor and evaluate OA policies' effects on biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective registration of trials at inception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective registration of trials at their inception is generally accepted as a means to prevent publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register trials before enrollment to create an unbiased sample of conducted studies, aid identification of unpublished studies, and reduce outcome reporting bias. Registries should be public, open to prospective registrations, and preferably managed by not-for-profit entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting studies based on pre-submitted protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting studies for publication mainly on the basis of their pre-submitted research protocol can help reduce publication bias by ensuring publication regardless of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Lancet assessed and registered selected trial protocols and committed to peer review the main clinical findings (though not necessarily to publish the final paper). This encourages adherence to pre-stated primary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepublication of protocols (systematic reviews and trials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing protocols before study completion allows feedback on methodology and question addressed and prevents duplication and outcome reporting bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cochrane Database publishes accepted review protocols after peer review. Electronic publication of protocols increases transparency so discrepancies between protocol and final report are detectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and content of clinical trial registries
rubrics_metrics.description: A clinical trial registry is 'a database of planned, ongoing or completed clinical trials... in which details concerning the trial’s objectives, main design features, sample size, and tested treatment are stored'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registries should include sufficient trial metadata to decide relevance and should be searchable by systematic reviewers. Important registries include ISRCTN and ClinicalTrials.gov; other national registries also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary registration is often incomplete; mandatory regulation may be needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary registration of clinical trials is often incomplete and a mandatory system by government regulation may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictions have used laws/regulations (e.g. Spain, FDA Modernisation Act) to require registries/ databases; consider advocating for or using data from mandatory registries when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: International standards and registries (WHO Registry Network)
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO has set international standards for clinical trial registration and operates a Registry Network and Trial Registry Portal to improve best practice and prevent selective dissemination by specific registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WHO portals and Clinical Trials Search Portal to identify registered trials across multiple registries; international harmonisation aids comprehensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE policy requiring trial registration before patient enrollment
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2005 ICMJE member journals require trials to be registered at or before the onset of patient enrolment in a public, open registry as a condition for consideration of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy markedly increased registrations (e.g. ClinicalTrials.gov spikes in 2005). Systematic reviewers should be aware that ICMJE-covered journals enforce this and register trials accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register trial results (summary results) to reduce outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of all trial results (published and unpublished) has been advocated to reduce publication and outcome reporting bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly available full summary results help reduce bias; debate continues about the scope and implementation, but reviewers should search for registered results in addition to registration records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend registration beyond phase III/IV to early-stage and non-trial studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective registration has mainly focused on phase III and IV trials; biased selection of early-stage trials and non-trial studies remains unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the potential bias introduced by under-registration of phase I/II, basic research, observational studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, and advocate or search for registries that include these study types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registries are useful only if reviewers search them and results are accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials registries will only reduce publication bias if systematic reviewers include registries in their search strategies and trial results are accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviewers must explicitly search trial registries, use registry-provided data, and follow up with trialists where studies are registered but not published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access policies by funders improve access for publicly funded research but may miss industry-sponsored studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory open access to results has been adopted by many funders, but current policies focus on non-industry-sponsored studies and cannot prevent biased reporting from industry-sponsored research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting reviews, be mindful that open access availability may be uneven across sponsor types; search other sources for industry results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-archiving may be selective and biased
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-archiving for open access is likely to be selective and may be biased; OA does not convincingly increase citations in all settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume self-archived literature represents an unbiased sample; include other search modalities to locate non-archived studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators' right to publish and limitations on sponsor veto
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should not allow sponsors veto power or sign confidentiality agreements that prevent dissemination of scientifically rigorous results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rennie recommended investigators should never allow sponsors veto power; institutions and researchers should avoid agreements that give sponsors control over publication or data access. Examine clinical trial agreements for clauses on IP and data control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research sponsors' guidelines and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders often require adherence to influential research guidelines (e.g. ICH Topic E6, EU Clinical Trial Directive, Declaration of Helsinki, CONSORT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dwan et al. found some funders emphasise publication of both positive and negative results and request adherence to trial protocols with explicit reporting of changes. Funders' guidelines should be used/strengthened to reduce selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confirmatory large-scale multicentre trials when publication bias is suspected
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory large-scale trials are generally less vulnerable to publication bias and may be conducted to provide more convincing evidence when publication bias cannot be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large trials can minimise impact of biases related to study design, selection of control, participants and setting. Systematic reviews of small studies can inform the need and design for large confirmatory trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public awareness and multi-stakeholder action to prevent publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide public awareness of the detrimental consequences of publication bias and actions by government, journals and research sponsors are first steps to prevention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote editorial policy changes, peer review transparency, disclosure of commercial interests, electronic publication, trial registration and open access; however, evidence on effectiveness of these measures remains limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensitivity and precision in literature searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Design searches that strike a balance between sensitivity (finding as many relevant studies as possible) and precision (limiting retrieval of irrelevant records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor higher sensitivity when missing studies would bias results, but be prepared to screen more records. Use methods (e.g. Bennett's methodology) to assess number of studies potentially missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit multiple searching modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on electronic bibliographic databases; use a range of searching modalities including citation tracking, hand-searching of journals and bibliographies, contacting experts, and searching grey literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting searches to a single or small set of modalities may miss non-significant studies in poorly indexed sources. Hand-searching and snowballing (reference and citation tracking) can identify additional eligible studies beyond protocol-driven searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design electronic search strategies for high sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic searches should be designed to ensure desired sensitivity by using multiple databases, combining text and index terms, avoiding overly specific limiting terms, and developing sensitive search filters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language restrictions where possible, favour generic search terms to maximise sensitivity, and be aware each database has partial coverage; combine searches across MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search grey literature and non-English-language sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference abstracts, company/regulatory reports, and non-English-language studies can be important sources; standard bibliographic searches may miss them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine how relevant societies publish abstracts; use Cochrane hand-searching programmes, search language-specific databases (e.g. LILACS), and check regulatory reviews (e.g. FDA) for unpublished reports. Recognise resource and language constraints when planning searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate ongoing and unpublished trials systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify ongoing or unpublished trials via trial registers, grey literature, internet searches, email surveys, and direct contact with investigators, acknowledging difficulties in distinguishing ongoing vs completed unpublished studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trial registers (ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN), carefully tailored web searches, targeted investigator contact (after hand-searching conference abstracts and review articles), and consider the low response rates and potential duplicate records across registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious including unpublished data from interested sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of unpublished data may not reduce bias if the data are provided by interested sources (e.g. industry), and identifying representativeness of unpublished trials is difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess provenance and potential conflicts of interest for unpublished data; attempt to determine whether identified unpublished trials represent the whole set of unpublished studies before assuming bias is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess risk of publication bias using study characteristics and quality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain study features (observational design, small sample size, small effect size) and study quality issues increase risk of publication bias; conflicts of interest are an important consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform comprehensive quality assessment to detect selection, performance, attrition and detection biases. Consider funding sources and competing interests; use Ioannidis' list of circumstances (small sample size, many tested relationships, analytic flexibility, financial interests, hot fields) as indicators of higher risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funnel plot and contour-enhanced funnel plots for detecting small-study effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot treatment effect against sample size or standard error: a funnel shape is expected if there is no publication bias; departures may indicate small-study effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard error (or inverse standard error) on the vertical axis as it accounts for event counts/variation. Contour-enhanced funnel plots add significance contours (e.g. p<0.01, p<0.05) to help determine whether missing studies lie in statistically significant regions, suggesting publication based on significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand selection mechanisms and interpret funnel plot asymmetry cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetry can arise from selection for statistical significance, sample size, direction of effect, or other selection rules; different selection mechanisms produce different funnel-plot patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider simulation examples: when true effect is zero, selection of significant small studies creates empty areas around zero; when true effect is small, missing small non-significant studies produce skewed plots with exaggerated effects in small studies. Interpret in context of likely selection processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of funnel plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Funnel plots require a range of study sizes, are informal and subjective, and asymmetry may be caused by factors other than publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise subjectivity and dependence on choice of effect measure (SE, variance, sample size, OR/RR). Alternative causes of asymmetry include clinical heterogeneity, methodological differences in small studies, inadequate analysis, fraud, choice of effect measure, and chance. Use funnel plots alongside other assessments.
